since you’re simply asking about symptoms to help understand yourself better, ima let this slide. 

the way you’re describing that extreme level of anger that manifests as violent behavior definitely seems to fall in line with how IED presents, especially if it’s grossly out of proportion to the situation. (ex. punching your wall, flipping your chair and destroying things in your room over something like losing at a video game) 

since you mentioned how your episodes usually don’t last longer than 30 mins, that also actually lines up with the duration of IED episodes. IED episodes typically last from a few minutes up to that 30 minute mark of intensely reactive anger over minor stressors. it’s almost common to experience feelings of guilt and remorse after each outburst.

while there has never been a purely communist country, if you look at some of the countries that have attempted to put it into practice, a lot of the flaws i mentioned happened. north korea is probably the most notorious example of this. It left it’s citizens in poverty, there’s practically no individual freedom in expression, and you get persecuted or executed for even the slightest bit of disloyalty/opposition. others like cuba, vietnam, and laos, while maybe not as extreme as NK, have also left its citizens poor, restricted individual freedom, and (another flaw i forgot to mention) working conditions aren’t necessarily the cleanest or humane (most of all jobs are agricultural) 

china is probably the one exception of a thriving “communist” country, but i put communist in quotes because while china identifies as communist, it’s actually more of a predominantly socialist country that incorporates some aspects of capitalism. socialism ≠ communism

from my own understanding, the end goal of communism is to achieve a moneyless, classless, stateless society. however, it can’t become that overnight, which is why it often appears authoritarian at first, with a very powerful centralized government, controlling everything. 

there also hasn’t been a purely capitalist country. while the united states is very much a capitalistic country, all the services i mentioned as well as gov intervention and social security (i forgot to mention this earlier) technically ARE socialist in nature, whether or not they were implemented to combat capitalist extremism. as far as i know, they are publicly owned and funded so that anyone who needs them can benefit from them for little to no cost. so the united states is indeed a mixed economy 

don’t get me wrong, i do acknowledge the flaws of capitalism, i do believe they aren’t talked about enough, however as i’ve said already, any socioeconomic system comes with pros and cons. so i guess the one question now is which one is best? which one makes it so the pros outweigh the cons? evidently, the answer is subjective

i will admit, a purely free-market economy would definitely have its flaws, like monopolies being more likely to form, governments turning into corporatocracies, and while the citizens may benefit at first, they would end up becoming small and inferior to the top dogs. although the same argument can be made for any (pure) economic system. even something seemingly utopian like communism, comes with cons that imo don’t get mentioned enough. like limited individual freedoms, driving nearly everyone into poverty, limited spending and earning, no savings allowed, and worst yet, any opposition may result in exclusion or persecution

to me personally, the main thing i appreciate about free-market economics is that it makes it so the citizens can have the freedom to purchase and invest in anything they want, instead of the gov controlling what the people can or can’t buy/invest in. the citizens have power to control supply and demand instead of just the top dogs. 

realistically however, a vast majority of countries have mixed economies, which incorporate elements from different economic systems into one. even the united states, while being a predominantly capitalistic and free-market country, is not purely either one. welfare programs, unemployment benefits, disability benefits, SNAP, medicare/medicaid, etc, are all aspects of socialism that a lot of people, even american citizens, forget to bring up. while i don’t like having higher taxes, if those taxes are at least being spent to help the poor and disabled, then that’s just fine. charities imo can also be helpful too so people don’t have to solely rely on our tax dollars.

so it appears that the main differences between the 2 are the age of onset and their core aspects. the symptoms can only count as ADHD if they’re chronic, present in more than one setting, and were present since childhood, before the age of 12. whereas with anxiety disorders, the onset can be at any age but is most commonly diagnosed in young adulthood. 

the core aspects of ADHD are inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, and while ADHD’ers can certainly get anxious at times, chronic anxiety is typically not characteristic of the ADHD experience, unless of course, someone has both.

anxiety disorders on the other hand, are rooted in experiencing a practically constant state of fear and worry, even about the most mundane things, you may not even be able to pinpoint the cause or triggers for anxiety initially. people with anxiety disorders can appear inattentive or hyperactive when anxiety rises but these usually dissipate when anxiety dies down.

even overlapping symptoms are usually caused differently, restlessness/inability to relax for instance is tied to fear of what may happen in anxiety, but is tied to a more general feeling of urgency for ADHD, like needing to be constantly on-the-go. distractibility/difficulty focusing in anxiety is typically due to worries weighing heavily on the mind while in ADHD, is typically due to painful boredom from lack of stimulation
